To fix (2)

To fix Codebook Check

What we found

We found no codebook or README documentation for the 412 extracted data columns.

Show details

This module checks whether each extracted data column is documented in a codebook or README, and flags documented variables that never appear in the data.

We examined 11 codebook/README/label sources and 412 data columns across 44 files.

No codebook or README documentation was found, so no data columns could be matched to variable definitions.

To fix Reproducibility Check

What we found

  • We assessed AND ran 55 Python code files for reproducibility.
  • 5 Python files skipped as byte-identical duplicates of another file already in the run.
  • 7 of 41 Python scripts ran without error when executed (13 more files are imported by other files, not run on their own).
  • 10 installable Python dependencies detected.

Note

See the section Reproducibility Check below for the details.

Absolute Paths

Best programming practice is to use relative file paths (e.g., ‘./files’) instead of absolute file paths (e.g., ‘C://Lakens/project_dir/files’) as these folder names do not exist on other computers. No absolute file paths were found in any of the code files.

Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid setwd() in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. No setwd() calls were found in any of the code files.

Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid install.packages() in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an renv.lock/DESCRIPTION for R, a requirements.txt for Python). No install.packages() calls were found in any of the code files.

Libraries / Imports

Best programming practice is to load all required libraries/imports in one block near the top of the code. In 17 code files, libraries/imports were at multiple places (i.e., with more than 3 non-comment lines in between).

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.

We examined 412 columns across 44 data files.

Issues Identified

14 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

About the personal-information flags. These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

  • Column names are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (email, telefoonnummer, geboortedatum, …). A column called phone_number flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
  • Values are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
  • Free text is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means look at this column. Where the data is already de-identified (an ip column reading Anonymized, a name column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

Careless Responding

No file could be screened for careless responding.

What this does not cover. Only 0 of 44 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

More detail

Ethics Approval Check

We did not detect an ethics approval statement, and this paper does not appear to involve live data collection from human or animal participants. Ethics approval is typically not required for theoretical work, simulations, reviews, meta-analyses, or secondary analyses of published data.

Power Analysis Check

No power analyses were detected.

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen’s d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

How Ethics Approval Check works

This module searches for statements of ethics approval, IRB approval, institutional review board approval, and related terms.

Patterns are designed to capture:

Human research committee names - Institutional Review Board / IRB (US standard) - Independent Ethics Committee / IEC (ICH-GCP international clinical trial term) - Ethical/Ethics Review Board (generic) - Ethics (Advisory/Review) Committee/Board/Panel/Sub-committee - Research Ethics Committee/Board/Panel (UK/Canada/Australia) - Medical Ethics Committee - Human Subjects/Research Committee / Human Research Ethics (Advisory) Panel - Committee for/on the Protection of Human Subjects - Committee on (Health) Research Ethics - Office of Research Ethics - Abbreviations: IEC, REC, REB, ERB, METC, DEC. REC/REB/ERB/DEC are short enough to collide with unrelated jargon (e.g. REC as a recognition-heuristic model abbreviation, DEC as a decision-task label, Reb as an author surname), so these four require an ethics/approval/committee/board/panel/institutional/ protocol word within ~30 characters in the same sentence. IRB and IEC are kept unconstrained as they are not observed to collide in practice. - Dutch: Medisch-ethische toetsingscommissie (METC) - French: Comité d'éthique / Comité d'Ethique

Animal research committee names - Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee / IACUC (US standard) - Any sentence containing animal(s) and committee (or board/panel) within ~5 words of each other — catches Experimental Animal Care and Use Committee, Animal Ethics Committee, Animal Welfare Board, Animal Welfare Ethical Review Body, etc. - UK: Animal Welfare Ethical Review Body / AWERB - Dutch: Dierexperimentencommissie / DEC (see DEC constraint above); Instantie voor Dierenwelzijn / IvD - German: Tierversuchskommission / TvK (advisory committee under §15 Tierschutzgesetz) - French: Comité d'éthique en expérimentation animale / CEEA; Comité d'éthique animale - Spanish: Comité de ética en experimentación animal / CEEA

Approval phrasing - Ethics/Ethical (approval|clearance) [was] (granted|obtained|received|given|secured) - Ethically approved - Approved by the (ethics|irb|institutional|independent|local|review|research) ... - This/The study/protocol/experiment/procedures/methods/research [was] (approved|reviewed) by - Study was ethically approved - (Followed|met|follow) the ethical (guidelines|standards|requirements) - In accordance with ... ethical (guidelines|standards) - Ethics protocol - Approved under (protocol|reference|number)

Waiver / exemption - Ethics/Ethical (waiver|exemption) - IRB (waiver|exemption|exempt) - Exempted from (ethics|irb|institutional review) - Waived by the (ethics|irb|institutional|review) (committee|board) - Deemed exempt

Declaration of Helsinki - Declaration of Helsinki / Helsinki Declaration

Patterns are NOT designed to capture: - General ethical considerations or ethical dilemmas in study content - Mentions of “ethics” in theoretical or philosophical contexts - Author approval of a manuscript (e.g. “all authors approved the final version”) - Ethical behaviour as a measured variable (e.g. “ethical decision-making”) - URLs containing “ethics” in path components

Live data collection is detected by the internal helper .detect_live_data(), which searches for sentences indicating that data were collected directly from human or animal participants. Papers without any live-data signal are not flagged as missing ethics approval. The helper uses conservative patterns to avoid flagging secondary data analyses, computational experiments, or economics papers that analyse existing survey data. See .detect_live_data() for the full list of patterns and intentional exclusions.

A paper that states that no human or animal subjects took part (“no human subjects were involved”, “did not involve human participants”, or people taking part “not as subjects”) is not expected to have an ethics statement, whatever participant phrase it also has (see .detect_no_participants()). A negation near a participant phrase alone (“No participants were excluded”) does not count: it reports a study with participants.

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Power Analysis Check works

This module uses regular expressions to identify sentences that contain a statistical power analysis. If specified by the user, it also uses a large language model (LLM) to extract information reported in power analyses, including the statistical test, sample size, alpha level, desired level of power, and magnitude and type of effect size.

The Power Analysis Check module uses regular expressions to identify sentences that contain a statistical power analysis. Without the use of an LLM, the module uses regular expressions to classify the power analysis as a-priori, sensitivity or post-hoc. With the use of an LLM, it checks if the power analysis is reported with all required information.

The regular expressions can miss power analyses, or fail to classify them correctly. The type of power analysis is often difficult to classify, which can easily be solved by explicitly specifying the type of power analysis as ‘a-priori’, ‘sensitivity’, or ‘post-hoc’. Note that ‘post-hoc’ or ‘observed’ power is rarely useful. The LLM can fail to identify information in the paper, and will not have access to information in paragraphs in the paper other than those that contain the word ‘power’. This package was validated by the Metacheck team on articles in Psychological Science.

This module was developed by Lisa DeBruine, Daniel Lakens and Cristian Mesquida

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 128 papers with 246 instances of power statements, 203 were correctly detected (true positives), 22 were missed (false negatives) and 21 were incorrectly detected (false positives). Overall, among all instances flagged as power statements, 90.6% were correct (positive predictive value).

How Preregistration Check works

Retrieve information from preregistrations in a standardised way, and make them easier to check.

The Preregistration Check module identifies preregistrations on the OSF and AsPredicted based on links in the manuscript, retrieves the preregistration text, and organizes the information into a template. The module retrieves text from the OSF with its API, and from AsPredicted with ResearchBox’s API when a ResearchBox key is set (see rbox_token()), or else from the preregistration’s web page. The information in the preregistration is returned. An AsPredicted link that could not be read is named in the report, with the reason.

The module can’t extract information from non-structured preregistration templates (i.e., where the preregistration is uploaded in a single text field) and it can’t retrieve information in preregistrations that are stored as text documents on the OSF.

If you want to extend the package to be able to download information from other preregistration sites, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Marginal Significance works

List all sentences that describe an effect as ‘marginally significant’.

The marginal module searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern. The list of terms is a subset of those listed in a blog post by Matthew Hankins. The module returns all sentences that match terms describing ‘marginally significant’ results.

Some of the terms identified might not be problematic in some contexts, and there are ways to describe ‘marginal significance’ that are not detected by the module.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 51 papers with 87 statements, this module correctly identified 38 statements (true positives) and incorrectly flagged 22 statements (false positives). It failed to detect 27 statements. Thus, among all statements flagged by the module, 63% were genuine cases (positive predictive value). However, the module missed 42% of all true statements (false negative rate).

How StatCheck works

Check consistency of p-values and test statistics

The Statcheck module runs Statcheck. Statcheck searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern, and identifies APA reported statistical tests. More information on the package can be found at https://github.com/cran/statcheck. The module only returns Statcheck results for t-tests and F-tests, as these are the only tests which have been validated, see https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv/tcxaj_v1/.

Statcheck was developed by Michèle Nuijten and Sascha Epskamp.

Statcheck considers p = 0.000 an error, as you should report p < 0.001. Furthermore, p < 0.03 is an error if the p-value was 0.031, and one should simply report exact p-values (p = 0.031). Statcheck might miss one-sided tests, and falsely assume the p-value is incorrect. For more information, see StatCheck.

This module only checks statistical results reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process statistics reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 685 tests with 34 instances of inconsistent reporting, Statcheck correctly detected 34 of them, and incorrectly identified 26. Therefore 0% of true instances were missed, and 43% of detections were false positives. See https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv/tcxaj_v1/ for more details of the validation.

How Exact P-Values works

List any p-values reported with insufficient precision (e.g., p < .05 or p = n.s.) or reported as exactly zero (e.g., p = .000).

This module uses regular expressions to identify p-values. It will flag any values reported as p > ? or p < numbers greater than .001. It will also flag p-values reported as exactly zero (e.g., p = .000, p = 0.00), which are mathematically impossible — p-values are never exactly zero and should instead be reported as p < .001.

A p-value that is not the result of a test is not flagged: a table note (“* p < .05, ** p < .01”), a figure legend (“Asterisks indicate significant differences (p < .05)”, “Values in bold are significant at p < .05”) or a stated threshold (“p < .05 was considered significant”, “thresholded at p < .001”). GROBID often puts such notes into the running text, so each p-value is judged by the words in its own clause (the text up to a “;” or a full stop), and never left out when a test statistic belongs to it (“F(1, 7) = 8.03, # p < .05”). The column not_a_test of the table says why a p-value was left out (“marker”, “threshold” or “legend”). Notes in other forms, such as a marker after the p-value (“p < .05 (*)“), are still flagged.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (“decreased at the p < .05 significance threshold”).

This module only checks p-values reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process p-values reported only in tables (as opposed to a table’s footnote text, which the module does see and tries to exclude — see above).

This module was developed by Lisa DeBruine and Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 225 papers containing 405 instances of non-exact p-values, the module correctly detected 269 cases (true positives) and incorrectly identified 78 (false positives). It missed 136 instances of imprecisely reported p-values (false negatives) and correctly identified 4557 cases of precisely reported p-values (true negative). Additionally, 78% of positive detections were correct (positive predictive value).

How Non-Significant P Value Check works

This module checks for imprecisely reported p values. If p > .05 is detected, it warns for misinterpretations.

The nonsignificant p-value check searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern. The module identifies all p-values in a manuscript and selects those that are not reported to be smaller than or equal to 0.05. It returns all sentences containing non-significant p-values.

In the future, the Metacheck team aims to incorporate a machine learning classifier to only return sentences likely to contain misinterpretations. If you want to help to improve the module, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module only checks p-values reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process p-values reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 194 papers with 1602 instances of non-significant p-values, this module correctly detected 1486 of them, and incorrectly identified 153. Additionally, 91% of detections were true instances (positive predictive value). That is, when this module flags non-significant p-values in a paper, it correctly identifies an issue 91% of the time.

How Effect Sizes in t-tests and F-tests works

The Effect Size module checks if effect sizes are correctly reported in t-tests and F-tests.

The Effect Size check searches for regular expressions that match typical ways in which effect sizes are reported. It subsequently checks different ways in which Cohen’s d, g, ηp2, and ωp2 can be computed against the reported value. If effects are missing, or might be incorrect, you the module provides a warning. The module was validated on APA reported statistical tests, and might miss effect sizes that were reported in other reporting styles. It was validated by the Metacheck team on papers published in Psychological Science.

This module only checks statistical results reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process statistics reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 161 papers with 1469 tests, this module correctly detected 1106 reported effect sizes (true positives) and correctly identified 295 cases where no effect size was present (true negatives). However, it missed 23 that were reported (false negatives), and incorrectly identified 45 effect sizes when none were reported (false positives). Among all instances detected by the module, 96% were true cases (positive predictive value). In a validation against 221 reported Cohen’s d effect sizes, it correctly indicated coherence in 218 cases (99%). In a validation against 485 partial eta-squared effect sizes, it correctly indicated coherence in 480 (99%)

How Codebook Check works

This module checks whether the data columns in a repository are documented in a codebook or README. It locates codebook/readme files, extracts the variable definitions they contain, matches those definitions against the data columns extracted by data_check, and reports documentation coverage: how many data columns are documented, and which documented variables are never used.

The Codebook Check module consumes the columns and file classification produced by data_check (and, transitively, repo_check). Files classified as codebook or readme are parsed with parse_codebook(), which reads structured tables (CSV/TSV/Excel with a variable-name column and a label column), embedded labels in haven files (SPSS/Stata/SAS), and plain text from rich-text formats (docx/pdf/rtf/odt). Embedded haven labels from data files are also harvested directly.

Each data column is then matched against the parsed variable definitions with match_column_labels(), using normalised-name matching with experiment-group scoping, haven-label priority, and rule-based label-equivalence merging.

Beyond the variable label, the module harvests the DDI-style per-variable properties a source supplies: the value labels / code list (the 1=“Strongly disagree”…5=“Strongly agree” mapping — from SPSS/Stata value labels and from a codebook “values”/“coding” column), the missing-value scheme (which codes denote missingness, from haven declared missings and labels that read as “refused”/“n/a”), and question text and columns when present. These are carried onto the matched data columns and exported into the Psych-DS variableMeasured (as a schema.org code list plus namespaced metacheck: fields).

The module defaults to rules-only when llm_use(FALSE). When llm_use(TRUE), three optional LLM tiers run: parsing unstructured codebook text that the rules could not handle, fuzzy-matching still-unlabelled columns to still-unmatched codebook variables, and merging conflicting label definitions into a single canonical label.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the codebook_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Repository Check works

This module retrieves information from repositories.

The Repository Check module lists files on the OSF, GitHub, ResearchBox, DSpace (PsychArchives and other legacy- and DSpace 7-based installations), Zenodo, Dataverse, Figshare, Dryad, ReShare, 4TU.ResearchData, Mendeley Data, DataONE (Arctic Data Center, KNB, and other member nodes), and LDbase based on links in the manuscript.

Listing a repository’s files never requires an API key, but some hosts answer faster or more completely with one: OSF allows 100 requests/hour unauthenticated versus 10,000/day with a token (see [osf_pat()]), and Dryad enforces a strict per-IP daily quota on repeated listing (see cache below). Dryad is a special case beyond rate limits: listing a Dryad dataset’s files works without a key, but actually downloading file CONTENTS from Dryad fails with HTTP 401 unless a key is set, even for a fully public dataset (see [dryad_pat()] or [dryad_auth()]). Since this module only lists files and never downloads their contents itself, that limitation applies to data_check and code_check (which do download content), not here – see their own documentation.

When a linked OSF page is a registration, its registered_from project (the one it was registered from, which the manuscript itself may never link directly) is also checked: if that project is public its files are listed under its own URL, and if it is closed or otherwise inaccessible the report flags it explicitly, since some registrations only describe their content rather than mirroring it.

If you want to extend the package to be able to download files from additional data repositories reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the repo_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Code Check works

This module retrieves information from repositories checked by repo_check about code files (R, Python, SAS, SPSS, Stata, Mplus, MATLAB).

The Code Check module checks R (also R Markdown and Quarto), Python (also Jupyter notebooks), SAS, SPSS, Stata, Mplus, and MATLAB files, using regular expressions to check the code; JASP files are listed but not read. The language of a Quarto document or a notebook is read from the file itself (its engine or kernel), not from its extension. The regular expression search will detect the number of comments, the lines at which libraries/imports are loaded, attempts to detect absolute paths to files, setwd() and install.packages() calls, and lists files that are loaded, and checks if these files are in the repository; R code is also parsed. The module will return suggestions to improve the code if there are no comments, if libraries/imports are loaded in lines further than 4 lines apart, if files that are loaded are not in the repository, if absolute file paths, setwd() or install.packages() are found, and if R code cannot be parsed.

The regular expressions can miss information in code files, or falsely detect parts of the code as a fixed file path. Libraries/imports might be loaded in one block, even if there are more than 3 intermittent lines. The module was tried out internally on papers published in Psychological Science, but has not been formally validated. There might be valid reasons why some loaded files can’t be shared, but the module can’t evaluate these reasons, and always gives a warning.

The module also checks whether the repository pins the R/package versions the analysis actually depended on: an renv.lock file (parsed for the R version and every locked package + its version/source), a sessionInfo()/sessioninfo::session_info() text dump (matched by filename — sessionInfo.txt/session_info.txt and similar, or embedded in a README), or a groundhog::groundhog.library()/checkpoint::checkpoint() date-pin call in the code (a bare library(groundhog)/library(checkpoint) does not count — the pinning call itself must be present). When none of these is found, the report flags it as a reproducibility gap: package versions may drift between when the analysis was run and any later reproduction attempt.

If you want to extend the package to perform additional checks on code files, or make the checks work on other types of code files, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

Checking code requires downloading its file contents. For a paper whose repository is on Dryad, this never succeeds unless a Dryad API key is set: Dryad requires one to download file bytes, even from a fully public dataset (listing the repository’s files does not need one). Without a key, every Dryad-hosted code file is listed but unchecked, and a warning naming Dryad and ?dryad_pat/?dryad_auth is included among the download failures recorded in the manifest.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Raphael Merz

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the code_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Data Check works

This module classifies the files in a repository into semantic types (data, codebook, code, software, output, supplemental, readme, asset, other) and, for tabular data files, extracts each column’s type and summary statistics.

The Data Check module consumes the file list produced by repo_check (or any files added via local_path). Each file is classified with rule-based heuristics layered over metacheck’s file_category() and file_types: file names matching README / codebook patterns win first, then an extension crosswalk, then format-locked extension overrides. For every file classified as tabular data that is available locally, the module reads the file head, describes each column with data_col_facets() and computes summary statistics for numeric columns. Every sheet of a spreadsheet that holds a table is read: a file with several such sheets has its columns under source_file = "file.xlsx [sheet]", and the sheet column names the sheet of any spreadsheet with several sheets; a sheet of notes or a codebook is treated as documentation when the file has another table. Following DDI, a column is described by orthogonal facets rather than a single type: representation (numeric/text/datetime/code — how it is stored), measurement_level (Stevens: nominal/ordinal/interval/ratio), concept (what it measures: reaction_time/age/gender/likert/id/…), role (identifier/measure/condition/timestamp), unit, and a quality state (ok/empty/constant). Concepts are detected by name+value rules (the demographic concepts via data_check_demographic()); when llm_use(TRUE) the model fills concepts and measurement levels the rules left blank. Qualtrics survey exports are recognised (data_check_is_qualtrics()): their extra header rows are stripped so columns type correctly, and the reserved response-metadata columns (StartDate, Duration, Finished, …) are tagged.

The module defaults to rules-only when llm_use(FALSE): columns the rules cannot resolve (ambiguous 3–20-unique integers, ambiguous character columns) fall back to continuous / text respectively. When llm_use(TRUE), ambiguous columns and unresolved file types (other) are sent to llm() for optional refinement, and every file is assigned a study group (ex1, pilot2, shared, …) so that multi-study repositories can be recognised (used by psychds_check). Without an LLM the study group is left NA (unknown).

Column extraction requires files to be readable from disk. Files fetched by repo_check from OSF/GitHub/etc. without a local copy (file_location is NA) are classified but not column-extracted; pass local_path to point at a downloaded copy of the repository.

For a paper whose repository is on Dryad, this means column extraction never happens unless a Dryad API key is set: Dryad requires one to download file bytes, even from a fully public dataset (dataset listing and metadata do not need one). Without a key, every Dryad file stays classified but un-downloaded, column_n is 0, and a warning naming Dryad and ?dryad_pat/?dryad_auth is included among the download failures. A one-time session message is also shown (see repo_check) the first time a Dryad dataset is encountered with no key set.

Every downloaded text file the authors wrote (code, settings, survey definitions such as Qualtrics .qsf files, documentation, outputs) is searched for keys: API keys, access tokens and private keys, which let anyone who downloads the file use a paid service at the authors’ cost. Of a tabular data file only the column names and first 3 rows of the table as read are searched: its values come from participants, but a key the authors set for a whole survey (as embedded data in a Qualtrics survey flow) is exported in every response. The search uses the rules of the secret scanner betterleaks (https://github.com/betterleaks/betterleaks, MIT licence) of high and medium confidence. A key found turns the traffic light red; the report and the keys table give its file, line and type, and only its beginning. Other files over 25 MB and binary files are not searched. A key is never tested with its provider. Every module’s result has any whole key replaced by “keyremoved” (see module_run()).

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Levi Baruch

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the data_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Reproducibility Check works

This module assesses whether a paper’s R and Python code can be run on its data. It works in two phases. The static phase (always run) collects the package dependencies the code declares, rewrites the data-file paths that do not work in the repository as the authors organised it, works out the order the scripts must run in, and diagnoses why any referenced input file is unavailable — reporting what a reproduction attempt would involve and where it is likely to break. The execution phase (opt-in, execute = TRUE) then actually runs the code: it copies the repository into a throwaway directory, optionally installs the declared dependencies into a throwaway library, runs each script in order in an isolated subprocess with a per-script timeout, and captures the outcome and full output of each run.

By default (execute = FALSE) the module does not run any code — it performs only static analysis: reading dependencies with the same extractors as code_check, finding the files the code references in the repository, and building a run-order dependency graph. It reports what would be installed and run rather than doing it.

When execute = TRUE, the module additionally runs the downloaded code on your machine — a deliberate, opt-in action gated behind that argument (callr is required for R code). Each script runs in an isolated subprocess so a crash cannot take down the R session; note this isolates crashes, not the filesystem or network. Installs (when install_missing = TRUE) and the throwaway run library never touch your main R library. Each script’s outcome is one of ran_ok, errored, timed_out, dependency_unavailable, not_parsed, run_by_source (an R script another script runs with source(), which is run only inside that script, since on its own it lacks the packages and objects the sourcing script sets up first), run_by_import (a Python file other files import, a module rather than a script, unless it has an if __name__ == "__main__": block), jags_model (a JAGS or BUGS model saved with an R extension, which another script reads) or not_r_content (a file that is not R at all, such as a JSON or HTML dump); these last two are not run and are not failures. python2 marks Python 2 code that was not run. With sandbox = "docker" such code runs with Python 2.7 (option metacheck.docker_image_py2; FALSE turns this off), which modifications records; it is never converted, since that can change results. defines_functions is a file that only defines functions, which is used, not run (table$used_by names the scripts that use it), and not_analysis is a file of software rather than of the analysis: a package’s code, tests, documentation or setup.py, a copy of a tool, a web application, a script a program wrote (table$not_analysis_why says which); neither is run or counted as a script. docker_failed means the container never started, which says nothing about the script, so it keeps the light from being green but does not make it red. needs_a_person is a script that stopped because it asks a person to choose a file or answer a question, or that starts an app, and needs_internet one that stopped because the network is off in a Docker run, or, with internet = TRUE, could not reach what it asked for; download_too_large is a script stopped for downloading more than the limits allow (see internet), and out_of_memory one that, or a program it started (such as a compiler), ran out of the memory each script may use. All four are treated the same way. not_downloaded is a script that stopped on a file the repository lists but that was not downloaded, such as one over max_file_size: it could not be tried, so it is not counted as a script that did not reproduce (summary_table$repro_not_downloaded_n counts them apart). not_read is a file metacheck could not read, so it was not run; the light is then not green, as the file may read and run on another computer, and table$error_message says why, naming a package that is installed but cannot be loaded on the computer that ran the check. empty is a file with nothing in it, which is not run or counted as a script. For a script that did not run through, table$error_message is its error, short (at most 300 characters): the error line of its output, which names a package that is not there, with the address it asked for when it needed the internet, or the time limit it reached; table$reason sorts it into a kind. A timeout means “still running at the cutoff”, not a failure, so raise timeout for legitimately long-running (e.g. Bayesian) scripts. dependency_unavailable means the script’s own package could not be installed from live CRAN, the CRAN Archive, or a named GitHub/URL source — an infrastructure limitation, not a defect in the paper’s code, so unlike errored/timed_out it does not force the traffic light red. The full stdout/stderr of every run is kept in the result’s run_results (the report shows it in per-script dropdowns, capped for readability). The traffic light reflects the STATIC readiness signals by default, but an execution error (errored/timed_out) does recolour it to red — a script that crashes on its own analysis is a genuine reproduction failure. A script that fails with could not find function is run once more with the library() calls the project’s other scripts make added at its top (or the one package that exports the function, or magrittr for %>%), and a script that then runs is reported as reproducible only after that repair.

Dependencies are reported name-only, with the source (CRAN, GitHub, or a base package already shipped with R) — static analysis of the code cannot know which version was used, and running against current package versions is itself informative: a break argues the authors should have pinned versions. When the repository does record versions, a run with recorded_versions = TRUE installs the packages the scripts load at those versions, but it does not change the R version, which remains a limitation of the check.

Run order is derived from read-after-write data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads must run first), source() edges, and numeric filename prefixes as a weak tie-breaker. Ambiguous orderings, dependency cycles, and inputs a script reads but that no earlier script produces (and that are not in the repository) are surfaced as warnings, since these are the situations most likely to make an otherwise-correct reproduction fail.

Python code (.py files, and notebooks and Quarto documents whose code is Python, from which the code is extracted first) goes through the same two phases, reported in its own “Python code” section. Each file is checked for syntax errors with Python’s own parser when a Python interpreter (python, or else python3) is available; dependencies are read from the import statements, with versions from a requirements.txt or pyproject.toml when there is one, and installed with pip; each script runs as its own python process (processx is required), so unlike R scripts, a name one script defines is not available to another. When no Python interpreter is available, the Python files are reported as not run and the R results are still returned. Statistics the Python scripts print are compared with the paper together with the R output and any self-reproducible output (JASP/jamovi, SPSS-Viewer, notebook outputs).

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How PubPeer Comments works

This module checks references and warns for citations that have comments on pubpeer (excluding Statcheck comments).

The PubPeer module uses the PubPeer API to check for each reference that has a DOI whether there are comments on the post-publication peer review platform. If comments are found, a link to the comments is provided. Comments by ‘Statcheck’ on PubPeer are ignored, see https://retractionwatch.com/2016/09/02/heres-why-more-than-50000-psychology-studies-are-about-to-have-pubpeer-entries/.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

For more information, see PubPeer.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How RetractionWatch works

This module checks references and warns for citations in the RetractionWatch Database.

The RetractionWatch Check module compares the reference list against studies in the RetractionWatch database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that the study was retracted, has an expression of concern, or a correction.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

It is possible the authors are already aware that a study was retracted, but the module can’t evaluate this.

The database can be manually updated with the rw_update function. For more information, see https://gitlab.com/crossref/retraction-watch-data.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Replication Check works

This module checks references and warns for citations of original studies for which replication or reproduction studies exist in the FLoRA database.

The Replication Check module compares the reference list against studies in the FLoRA (FORRT Library of Replication Attempts) database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that a replication or reproduction of the original study exists, and should be cited. No reminder is given when the paper already cites that replication or reproduction (matched by its DOI).

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

It is possible the original study was cited for other reasons than the empirical claim tested, or that the replication/reproduction in the FLoRA database is for only one of the studies in the paper, and not the study the authors discuss.

The database can be manually updated with the FLoRA_update() function. For more information, see https://forrt.org/FLoRA/.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens, Lisa DeBruine and Lukas Wallrich

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Full text

Abstract

ClinicalTrials.gov provides valuable information for vaccine research, but fragmented data structures and inconsistent vaccine naming complicate systematic cross-trial analysis. The Study-Experiment-Assay Common Data Model (SEA-CDM) provides a standardized structure for biomedical study data, while biomedical ontologies supply semantic relationships among concepts. We extracted 9,147 vaccinerelated study records from the Aggregate Analysis of ClinicalTrials.gov (AACT) database, mapped their records into SEA-CDM, and linked vaccine products and reported adverse events (AEs) to the Vaccine Ontology (VO) and Ontology of Adverse Events (OAE), respectively. Building on the existing Ontology-based SEA Network (OSEAN), we organized the integrated data into relational tables and a Neo4j knowledge graph while retaining links to original registrations. We evaluated three applications to assess semantic trial retrieval, context-aware AE ranking and trial similarity, and trial design recommendation. First, VO-based query expansion retrieved 41 candidate RNA vaccine trials compared with 16 using exact VO identifier matching. Second, a context-aware AE ranking model incorporating SEA-CDM features and VO-derived vaccine families improved recall@10 from 0.317 to 0.383 over a frequency-based baseline. TransE and CompGCN embeddings achieved Hits@10 of 0.950 and 0.946, respectively, for retrieving trials sharing the same VO identifier within disease-specific candidate sets. Third, an ontology-based clinical trial design recommendation model was developed using several machine learning methods under leave-one-Material-out evaluation across 23 vaccine classes, although performance varied across classes. These findings demonstrate how structural and semantic integration can support multiple clinical trial analyses using vaccine studies as a case study. This framework provides a foundation for extending ontology-supported data integration and analysis to other clinical research domains.

1. Introduction

ClinicalTrials.gov provides valuable information for vaccine clinical trial research, including vaccine products, study designs, participant characteristics, and reported adverse events (AEs). Researchers and vaccine developers often need to identify relevant historical trials, compare reported AEs across similar studies, and examine previously registered trial designs. The Aggregate Analysis of ClinicalTrials.gov (AACT) database makes these data available in a relational format [1, 2]. However, relevant information is distributed across multiple tables, and vaccine products are often recorded as free text, making systematic data integration and cross-trial analysis challenging. Without standardized vaccine identifiers and explicit biological relationships, identifying similar vaccines often relies on text matching or computational similarity measures that may not capture their underlying biological connections. Biomedical ontologies provide standardized concepts and relationships that support semantic data integration and analysis, following principles promoted by initiatives such as the OBO Foundry [3] and FAIR data management practices [4]. The Vaccine Ontology (VO) systematically represents vaccine products, vaccine types, and their biological relationships, covering licensed vaccines, investigational vaccines, and vaccines evaluated in animal models [5] [6] [7]. For example, an RNA vaccine and a more specific COVID-19 RNA vaccine may have different VO identifiers, but their hierarchical relationship allows related trials to be retrieved together. VO is also linked to the Vaccine Investigation and Online Information Network (VIOLIN), a curated vaccine knowledge base that provides additional product information and stable vaccine identifiers [8, 9]. However, mapping free-text vaccine names from clinical trial records to VO remains challenging and has motivated the development of specialized natural language processing approaches [10]. Similarly, the Ontology of Adverse Events (OAE) provides standardized representations and hierarchical relationships for adverse events reported following medical interventions, including vaccination [11] [12] [13]. Together, VO and OAE provide a semantic foundation for organizing vaccine products and reported AEs.

While biomedical ontologies support semantic standardization, they do not by themselves provide a unified structure for organizing all components of clinical trial records. Existing common data models, such as the OMOP Common Data Model developed within the Observational Health Data Sciences and Informatics (OHDSI) community, primarily support the standardization of observational healthcare data [14, 15]. In contrast, ClinicalTrials.gov contains heterogeneous registry information, including study protocols, interventions, eligibility criteria, and reported results, which presents additional challenges for secondary analysis [16]. Previous studies have demonstrated the value of knowledge graphs and embedding-based approaches for clinical trial retrieval and recommendation [17, 18]. However, previous approaches have not typically integrated vaccine-specific ontology relationships with a standardized clinical trial data model to support multiple downstream applications within a unified framework.

The ontology-supported Study-Experiment-Assay Common Data Model (SEA-CDM) is a newly proposed cross-domain common data model that provides a standardized schema for integrating biomedical study evidence across domains [19]. SEA-CDM consists of 10 core tables and three accessory tables, providing a relatively compact schema for biomedical data integration. The advantage of SEA-CDM has been verified using vaccine transcriptomics data [19]. AACT organizes ClinicalTrials.gov records across 51 tables, requiring joins across multiple tables for certain cross-trial analyses, which makes query and analysis difficult. For example, identifying adverse events reported in trials involving related RNA vac-cines may require linking intervention, trial arm, and adverse event records across multiple AACT tables, while also accounting for inconsistent vaccine names. In the proposed framework, these records are organized into linked SEA-CDM entities and grounded to VO and OAE concepts, allowing related vaccine trials and their reported adverse events to be retrieved through ontology-based queries rather than exact text matching alone. We hypothesized that integrating vaccine clinical trial data with SEA-CDM and biomedical ontologies could facilitate systematic data integration, semantic querying, and downstream machine learning analysis.

To address the above hypothesis, we developed an automated pipeline to extract vaccine-related clinical trial records from AACT, map them into SEA-CDM, and link vaccine products and reported AEs to VO and OAE, respectively. Building on the previously established Ontology-based SEA Network (OSEAN) framework [19], we organized the integrated vaccine clinical trial data into relational and knowledge graph representations. We evaluated three complementary applications: (i) query-using VO expansion to retrieve related vaccine trials and examine OAE-grounded AE information; (ii) similarity and prediction-combining SEA-CDM context and VO-derived information for AE ranking, together with knowledge graph embeddings for trial similarity analysis; (iii) clinical trial design recommendation-using ontology-based similarity to identify relevant historical trials and suggest registered design characteristics. Together, these applications demonstrate how a standardized clinical data model and biomedical ontologies can be integrated to support multiple types of vaccine clinical trial analysis.

2. Materials and Methods

Figure 1 illustrates the overall workflow of this study. First, vaccine-related clinical trial records were extracted from the AACT relational database [1, 2]. The extracted records were then converted into SEA-CDM to provide a standardized representation of clinical trial information. Vaccine products and platforms were mapped to the Vaccine Ontology (VO), with VIOLIN product identifiers used when available, while reported adverse events (AEs) were mapped to the Ontology of Adverse Events (OAE). Clinical-Trials.gov identifiers (NCT IDs) were retained to link the integrated data to their original trial records. The resulting database and knowledge graph supported three downstream applications: ontology-based query, similarity and AE ranking, and clinical trial design recommendation. All analyses were based on the SEA-CDM AACT vaccine remapped v1.4 dataset, containing 9,147 studies from the AACT snapshot dated April 12, 2026, and the VO release dated June 12, 2026.

2.1 Data conversion using ontology-based SEA-CDM Vaccine trial selection and inclusion criteria.

Vaccine-related clinical trial records were identified from the local AACT pipe-delimited export using a predefined keyword-based filtering procedure implemented in the VaxCT preprocessing pipeline. Studies were included if at least one case-insensitive, whole-word match to a vaccine-or immunization-related term was found in any of three AACT fields: studies.brief_title, interventions.name, or keywords.name. The term list included general vaccine and immunization terms (e.g., vaccine, vaccination, immunization, and immunisation), as well as selected product-, platform-, and disease-related terms (e.g., mRNA, pneumococcal, HPV, and BCG). The complete keyword list is provided in Table S1. Matching was performed using word-boundary regular expressions to reduce unintended substring matches. The final cohort was defined as the union of NCT identifiers retrieved from the three fields. All AACT tables required for subsequent SEA-CDM mapping were restricted to the selected NCT identifiers.

No additional requirement for an identified investigational vaccine product was imposed during cohort selection. Therefore, some included studies may lack a specific product-level VO mapping. The final NCT cohort and the filtering procedure were retained to support reproducibility.

SEA-CDM construction.

SEA-CDM provides a standardized structure for organizing biomedical study information into defined entities and relationships, including Study, Experiment, Intervention, Material, Subject, Group, Occurrence, and Result [19]. SEA-CDM adopts a study-centered structure that explicitly organizes interventions, participant groups, and reported outcomes. This structure is particularly useful for representing ClinicalTrials.gov records, where trial design information and reported results must be integrated within a common framework.

We adapted this structure to represent the selected vaccine-related clinical trial records from AACT. Each included ClinicalTrials.gov registration was represented as a Study identified by its NCT ID, with the associated registry context organized under Experiment. Identifiable investigational vaccine products were represented as SEA-CDM Material entities, with each mapped vaccine product linked to a primary VO identifier. Vaccination procedures were represented as Intervention entities. Eligibility and demographic information were organized under Subject, trial arms under Group, and reported adverse events under Occurrence. Study design and protocol information was also retained as additional attributes for downstream analysis. Assay and Sample entities remained in the schema for compatibility with the original SEA-CDM model, although these data were less frequently available in ClinicalTrials.gov records and were not required for the primary analyses (Figure 2).

The integrated records were represented in relational SEA-CDM tables and an NCT-linked knowledge graph implemented using Neo4j [20]. The relational representation supports structured SQL queries, while the knowledge graph enables the exploration of relationships among trial entities and ontology concepts. Additional study characteristics, including disease, phase, study purpose, participant demographics, administration route, dosage, and VO mappings, were retained for downstream analyses. Feature sources are summarized in Table S2, while resource counts and OAE coverage are provided in Section S3.

VO/OAE grounding and ontology graph integration.

To provide standardized semantic representations, vaccine products and reported AEs were linked to their corresponding ontology concepts. VO organizes vaccine products and types through hierarchical and role-based relationships, including subClassOf and has_role [5, 6]. VIOLIN provides additional curated vaccine product identifiers, such as VIOLIN_5784 for Comirnaty, which can support the mapping of registry vaccine names to VO concepts [8].

Similarly, OAE provides standardized classes and hierarchical relationships for adverse events [11, 12]. Reported AE terms were mapped to OAE identifiers using label and synonym matching, supplemented by manually defined mappings for selected ambiguous terms, such as pyrexia to fever AE. In our pipeline, each identified investigational vaccine product was assigned a primary VO identifier and, where applicable, a broader vaccine platform identifier. Details of the vaccine-to-VO mapping audit and subsequent corrections are provided in Section S8. Importantly, the integrated knowledge graph incorporated not only the mapped VO and OAE identifiers but also their surrounding ontology relationships. Vaccine products were linked to VO classes, while reported AE terms were linked to OAE classes through SEA-CDM Occurrence records. The ontology hierarchy was preserved through relations such as subClassOf, allowing related vaccine categories and AE concepts to be explored within the same knowledge graph. This integrated representation supported the three downstream applications.

2.2 Use case 1 -Query

Use Case 1 focuses on retrieving vaccine clinical trials and their reported adverse events (AEs) using the integrated SEA-CDM data. We implemented two query approaches: exact VO identifier matching (Layer A) and ontology-based expansion (Layer B).

Layer A (Exact VO identifier matching).

In Layer A, trials are retrieved by matching the primary VO identifier assigned to an investigational vaccine product (arch_vo = v). Related SEA-CDM entities, including Intervention, Subject, Group, and Occurrence, are then used to examine reported AEs and filter trials by characteristics such as administration route, age, sex, or trial arm. When an AE term is successfully mapped to OAE, its standardized OAE identifier and label are displayed alongside the number of matching trials.

Layer B (Ontology-based expansion).

Unlike exact matching, Layer B considers related vaccine classes connected through VO relationships. For example, a query for RNA vaccines can also retrieve trials assigned to more specific classes, such as COVID-19 RNA vaccines. Instead of requiring arch_vo = v, the query expands the selected VO class to include related ontology concepts. Let N ↑ (v) denote ancestor classes and role-related peers, and D ↓ (v) denote descendant classes up to depth three, with sibling expansion disabled by default:

Trials are included when their VO identifiers belong to the expanded set E(v). Exact VO identifier matching (arch_vo = v) serves as the comparison baseline.

Both approaches support five query patterns: forward, reverse, compare, drill-down, and conditional queries. For AE ranking, the frequency of an AE term a is calculated as: trial_count(a; E) = |{t ∈ T (E) : a is reported on t}|, where T (E) represents the set of trials satisfying the VO identifier filter and any additional Intervention, Subject, or Group constraints. These counts represent the number of matching trials reporting each AE, rather than predicted AE incidence rates. Representative results for exact VO identifier queries and ontology-expanded queries are provided in Table S6 and Table 1, respectively.

2.3 Use case 2 -Similarity and prediction

Use Case 2 evaluates two complementary tasks using the integrated OSEAN data: context-aware AE ranking and knowledge graph-based trial similarity.

AE ranking (primary task).

The goal of AE ranking is to identify which adverse events are most likely to be reported in a given trial context. Each example corresponds to an NCT × Group-arm context x, associated with a set of reported AE terms Y x . Contexts were restricted to NCT × vaccine/control arms with at least one reported AE in the SEA-CDM Occurrence records; from these arms we used the 80 most frequent AE terms that each appeared in at least 25 contexts, yielding 2,571 contexts. The data were divided into training (80%) and testing (20%) sets by study, ensuring that all arms from the same trial were assigned to the same split.

We compared two models. Model A ranks AEs according to their overall frequency in the training data, producing the same ranking for all trial contexts. Model B generates context-specific AE rankings using vaccine family and SEA-CDM study characteristics. These models are defined as: where m(x) represents the vaccine's primary VO identifier and C(x) includes administration route, dosage, sex, age, trial arm role, and disease indication.

The vaccine family is derived from VO relationships, including subClassOf and has_role, which connect specific vaccine products to broader platform categories. Model B uses one-vs-rest logistic regression [21].

Reported and predicted AE terms were linked to OAE identifiers when mappings were available (78 of 80 terms). These mappings support interpretation of the results but are not used as prediction features. Model performance was evaluated using recall@10: where Y (10) x represents the ten highest-ranked predicted AE terms.

This metric measures the proportion of reported AEs recovered among the top ten predictions.

Trial similarity (secondary task).

To identify related vaccine trials, we generated study embeddings from the SEA-CDM and VO knowledge graph using TransE [22] and CompGCN [23]. Trial similarity was calculated using cosine similarity between study embeddings. For each query trial, candidate trials were ranked according to their embedding similarity, with trials sharing the same VO identifier considered relevant neighbors.

After joining the analysis cohort to VO-mapped vaccine products, 556 studies were available for embedding-based similarity. Evaluation used disease-specific candidate sets (other studies with the same disease indication): queries without a usable same-disease candidate set were excluded, leaving 541 queries. We reported Hits@1, Hits@10, and Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR). Hits@K measures the proportion of queries for which at least one relevant trial appears among the top K ranked candidates, while MRR summarizes the reciprocal rank of the first relevant trial. A VO-only edge ablation is provided in Section S5. Although OAE relationships were included in the integrated knowledge graph for AE-related analysis, they were not required for these trial similarity evaluations.

2.4 Use case 3 -Design recommendation

We developed an ontology-based clinical trial design recommendation model that identifies similar historical trials and uses their registered designs to recommend design characteristics. The model predicts four design fields: allocation, masking, intervention model, and enrollment size category. Recommendations are based on disease, study phase, study purpose, and vaccine product and platform VO identifiers.

For each query trial, the system identifies the top 20 most similar training trials and predicts each design field through a similarity-weighted vote. The design fields serve as prediction targets rather than input features or graph edges.

Neighbor scoring.

The similarity between a query trial q and a historical trial j is calculated as: S(q, j) = f ∈{disease,phase,purpose} w f 1 x f (q) = x f (j) + w plat s plat (q, j) + w mat s mat (q, j).

We assigned weights of 1 to disease and phase, 0.5 to study purpose, 1 to platform similarity, and 0.5 to vaccine-class similarity.

We compared exact identifier matching with ontology-based similarity. Exact matching assigns a similarity of 1 when two VO identifiers are identical and 0 otherwise:

Ontology-based similarity (OntSim) instead measures the overlap between the VO neighborhoods of two vaccine or platform VO classes using Jaccard similarity: where N (•) represents the set of related ontology concepts obtained through subClassOf and has_role relationships.

Identical identifiers receive a similarity score of 1.

Unlike exact matching, OntSim allows related vaccine classes with different VO identifiers to contribute to the recommendation. Disease, phase, and purpose matching remain the same for both approaches.

The final prediction for each design field is determined by a similarity-weighted vote among the top 20 neighbors.

Evaluation.

We used two evaluation strategies to assess performance under different scenarios: prediction for future trials and generalization to previously unseen vaccine classes.

Chronological evaluation (past to future).

Trials with start dates before 2022 were used for training, while trials starting in 2022 or later were used for testing (n=283). This evaluation simulates using historical trial information to recommend designs for future studies. Because many VO identifiers assigned to test trials were already represented in the training data, exact matching and ontology-based similarity could identify similar neighbors with identical VO identifiers.

Leave-one-Material-out (LOMO) evaluation.

To assess generalization to previously unseen vaccine classes, we evaluated 23 ontology-connected vaccine classes, each defined by a primary VO identifier.

In each round, all trials assigned to one vaccine class were excluded from training and used for evaluation (Section S4). Under this setting, exact matching cannot identify training trials with the same VO identifier, whereas OntSim can retrieve trials involving related vaccine classes through VO relationships. This evaluation therefore examines whether ontology relationships provide additional information when exact VO identifier matches are unavailable.

The reference labels were obtained from registered clinical trial designs. Accordingly, the recommendations reflect historical design choices rather than clinically optimal designs. Additional baseline methods and a prototype user interface are presented in Section S2 and Figure S1. The main results are presented in Table 4 and Figure 6.

3. Results

The integration of vaccine clinical trial records produced a standardized SEA-CDM resource with ontology-grounded study information. From 579,828 AACT study registrations, 9,147 vaccine-related studies were identified and mapped into SEA-CDM, yielding 18,294 Experiment records, 20,001 Intervention records, 9,147 Subject records, 617,510 Occurrence records, and 1,525,757 Result records. Among 14,190 distinct registry-reported AE terms, 5,040 were mapped to OAE concepts. The resulting relational database and knowledge graph provided a shared representation for the three downstream applications.

3.1 Query: Ontology expansion beyond exact VO identifier matching

VO-based query expansion retrieved more RNA vaccine trials than exact VO identifier matching. Using RNA vaccines (VO_0000186) as an example, exact matching identified 16 trials, whereas ontology expansion retrieved 41 candidate trials, including 25 additional trials (Figure 3). Exact matching retrieves only trials assigned to the queried VO identifier, while ontology expansion also includes trials mapped to related vaccine classes. Table 1 presents representative trials identified only through ontology expansion. Among the 25 additional records, 20 were mapped to the COVID-19 RNA vaccine class (VO_0005198), and five were mapped to the mRNA-loaded autologous dendritic cell vaccine class (VO_0007132). These trials were not retrieved through exact matching because their stored VO identifiers differed from the queried RNA vaccine identifier. The complete list of additional trials is provided in Table S8.

To illustrate how trial context influences AE ranking, Table 3 presents a Comirnaty-style query using the nucleic-acid vaccine family, intramuscular administration, COVID-19 indication, and adult participants. Compared with Model A, Model B moved upper respiratory tract infection from rank 5 to rank 2, diarrhoea from rank 10 to rank 4, and injection site pain from rank 11 to rank 6, while headache remained the highest-ranked AE. This example illustrates how incorporating vaccine family and structured trial characteristics changes the predicted AE ranking relative to overall reporting frequency. The Model B scores are used for ranking and should not be interpreted as clinical AE incidence probabilities.

3.3 Design recommendation

Ontology-based similarity modestly improved design recommendation for previously unseen vaccine classes under leave-one-Material-out (LOMO) evaluation. We evaluated 23 ontology-connected vaccine classes, excluding all trials from one vaccine class during each training round. While Exact could still identify historical trials with similar disease, phase, and study purpose, OntSim additionally used VO relationships to identify related vaccine classes with different VO identifiers. Averaging accuracy equally across the 23 vaccine classes, OntSim achieved 0.646 compared with 0.633 for Exact (Δ = +0.013), indicating a modest improvement when identical VO identifier matches were unavailable. In a separate chronological evaluation, OntSim and Exact achieved similar field-mean accuracy (0.664 versus 0.661), while HistGBDT achieved 0.664 (Table S3).

The effect of ontology-based similarity on design recommendation varied across vaccine classes (Figure 6). OntSim improved accuracy for 11 classes, decreased accuracy for seven classes, and produced little or no change for five classes (median Δ = 0). The largest improvement was observed for autologous tumor cell vaccines (Δ = +0.125). These results suggest that ontology-based similarity can improve design recommendation when related vaccine classes share similar design characteristics, but may reduce accuracy when their historical trial designs differ.

In contrast, OntSim showed the largest decrease in accuracy for RNA vaccines (VO_0000186; n = 13; ∆ = -0.038). Although Exact could still identify historical trials using disease, phase, and purpose, OntSim assigned higher similarity scores to some ontology-related vaccine classes with different enrollment patterns, including certain pneumococcal and DNA vaccine trials. These differences led to incorrect enrollment predictions in some cases. Complete per-class evaluation results are provided in Table S4.

To illustrate how ontology relationships affect individual design recommendations, we examined NCT00799110, a trial assigned to the autologous tumor cell vaccine class (VO_0007319), under LOMO evaluation. Both Exact and OntSim correctly predicted allocation, masking, and intervention model, but they differed in enrollment prediction. Exact predicted 50-149 participants, whereas OntSim correctly predicted fewer than 50 participants (Table 4). OntSim retrieved supporting GVAX vaccine trials with related but different VO identifiers (Table S7), illustrating how ontology-based relationships can provide additional evidence when exact VO identifier matches are unavailable.

4. Discussion

This study demonstrates how integrating vaccine clinical trial data into an ontology-supported SEA-CDM framework can support three complementary applications: trial retrieval, AE ranking, and vaccine clinical trial design recommendation. By combining the standardized data structure of SEA-CDM with semantic relationships from VO and OAE, OSEAN provides a unified resource for organizing and analyzing vaccine clinical trial information. Our results highlight the potential benefits of ontology-based integration while also showing that these benefits depend on the specific analytical task.

In Use Case 1, ontology-based query expansion enabled the retrieval of trials associated with related vaccine classes beyond exact VO identifier matching. This demonstrates the value of incorporating explicit semantic relationships into clinical trial queries. However, broader retrieval also depends on accurate ontology mappings, as incorrect assignments may introduce unrelated trials.

In Use Case 2, integrating SEA-CDM study characteristics with VO-derived vaccine families improved AE ranking compared with a frequency-based baseline. SEA-CDM provides structured trial context, including administration routes, participant characteristics, and disease indications, while VO contributes standardized vaccine classifications and biological relationships. Their combination enables contextaware AE ranking that captures information beyond overall reporting frequency, demonstrating the complementary value of structural and semantic integration. OAE further supports standardized interpretation of reported AEs. Knowledge graph embeddings also enabled the retrieval of trials sharing VO identifiers within the evaluated candidate sets.

In Use Case 3, ontology-based similarity provided modest improvements in design recommendation when identical VO identifier matches were unavailable, although performance varied across vaccine classes. However, this advantage was not observed in a separate pooled-holdout evaluation, where OntSim and Exact both achieved a trial-mean accuracy of 0.646 (Table S5). This suggests that the benefits of ontology-based similarity depend on the evaluation setting. This highlights that biologically related vaccine classes do not necessarily share similar trial designs. Differences in disease indications, development stages, and public health circumstances may influence enrollment strategies beyond what ontology-based similarity captures. Such contextual differences may help explain the lower performance observed for RNA vaccines, although this explanation was not directly evaluated.

Compared with previous clinical trial knowledge graph studies, our approach emphasizes the integration of structured trial information and explicit ontology relationships to support multiple downstream analyses. Chen et al. [17] developed the Clinical Trials Knowledge Graph (CTKG) to support trial similarity search and drug repurposing through graph embeddings. While their evaluation focused on embeddingbased retrieval, our integration of SEA-CDM with VO and OAE additionally supports ontology-based retrieval across related vaccine classes and context-aware AE analysis, demonstrating capabilities beyond similarity search alone. Devarakonda et al. [18] used knowledge graph embeddings and semantic inductive inference to recommend clinical trial elements, with performance evaluated primarily through textual similarity. In contrast, our approach predicts structured trial design fields and explicitly evaluates the contribution of ontology relationships when identical VO identifier matches are unavailable.

Previous work on vaccine ontology mapping and biomedical data integration established complementary foundations for our clinical trial applications. Li et al. [10] developed language model-based methods for mapping vaccine names to VO concepts, addressing the challenge of semantic standardization. Our study extends beyond concept mapping by incorporating ontology relationships into structured clinical trial data to support querying, prediction, and design recommendation. Huffman et al. [19] established SEA-CDM and OSEAN for integrating heterogeneous biomedical experimental data with ontology support, primarily demonstrating their application to immune-response studies. Building on this foundation, we extend the approach to clinical trial registry data and evaluate its utility across three complementary analytical applications.

The main contribution of this study is to demonstrate how the structured representation of SEA-CDM and the semantic relationships of biomedical ontologies can be jointly applied to clinical trial registry data, using vaccine clinical trials as a case study. Across three applications, this integration enabled broader ontology-based trial retrieval and improved context-aware AE ranking, while ontology-based similarity provided modest, evaluation-dependent benefits for design recommendation when exact Material matches were unavailable.

Our findings are subject to limitations related to retrospective data selection, registry-reported AE information, and the generalizability of the evaluation settings. First, our analyses relied on a retrospective AACT snapshot and keyword-based vaccine trial identification, which may have included unrelated studies or excluded relevant trials. In addition, incomplete or inaccurate VO/OAE mappings may affect ontology-based retrieval and analysis. Second, AE ranking was based on registry-reported AE terms rather than standardized incidence rates. Therefore, the predicted rankings should not be interpreted as clinical risk estimates or causal effects. Future studies could incorporate individual-level data from clinical trials and electronic health records to investigate associations between vaccine characteristics, administration routes, and AE occurrence. SEA-CDM could continue to provide a standardized structure for integrating these heterogeneous data sources, while VO and OAE could support semantic harmonization of vaccine exposures and adverse event outcomes, enabling more systematic risk factor analysis. Third, model performance and generalizability depend on the evaluation settings. Trial similarity was assessed using restricted candidate sets and shared VO identifiers as the relevance criterion, while design recommendation was evaluated on selected ontology-connected vaccine classes. The chronological evaluation used a later data snapshot and ontology release rather than a fully historical environment. Furthermore, the recommendation model has not been prospectively validated, and its outputs reflect historical trial designs rather than clinically established optimal choices.

5. Conclusion

In this study, we integrated vaccine clinical trial data into an ontology-supported SEA-CDM framework, combining standardized study information with semantic relationships from VO and OAE. The resulting OSEAN resource supports three complementary applications: ontology-based trial retrieval, contextaware adverse event ranking and trial similarity analysis, and clinical trial design recommendation. Our findings demonstrate that ontology relationships can improve the retrieval of related vaccine trials and support design recommendation, particularly when identical VO identifiers are unavailable, although performance varies across vaccine classes. By preserving links to the original ClinicalTrials.gov records, the framework provides traceable evidence for downstream analysis and decision support. Future work will focus on improving VO/OAE mapping coverage and accuracy, evaluating the additional contribution of OAE relationships to AE ranking, and assessing the framework through user-oriented evaluations.

3.2 Similarity and prediction: context-aware AE ranking

Combining SEA-CDM study characteristics with VO-derived vaccine families improved AE ranking compared with a frequency-based baseline. Model A produces the same AE ranking for all trials, whereas Model B adjusts the ranking based on vaccine family, administration route, disease indication, and other study characteristics. Model B achieved a recall@10 of 0.383, compared with 0.317 for Model A (Δ = +0.066; Table 2). This means that Model B recovered a larger proportion of reported AEs among its top 10 predictions for each trial context than the frequency-based baseline.

Knowledge graph embeddings effectively retrieved trials sharing VO identifiers within the evaluated disease-specific candidate sets. Across 541 queries, TransE and CompGCN achieved Hits@10 values of 0.950 and 0.946, respectively, indicating that at least one trial sharing the query's VO identifier appeared among the top 10 candidates for approximately 95% of queries (Table 2). TransE achieved an MRR of 0.710, compared with 0.688 for CompGCN. A VO-only edge ablation is presented in Section S5. 4 and 5). VO features showed the largest aggregate coefficient magnitude, followed by study indication and intervention features (Figure 4). Positive coefficients indicate higher predicted scores for the corresponding AEs in a given trial context, whereas negative coefficients indicate lower scores.
